sentences.text: Here’s where the two rule books split, and it’s a favorite exam question.
The Inland version of Rule nine adds a special rule for the Great Lakes, the Western Rivers, and other waters the Coast Guard specifies.
You won’t find it in the International rules.
On those waters, a power-driven vessel heading downbound with a following current has the right of way over an upbound vessel.
This is one of the very few places where the rules actually use those words.
The downbound vessel proposes the manner and place of passage.
And she initiates the maneuvering signals.
The upbound vessel, the one working against the current, holds as necessary to permit safe passing.
Think about a towboat pushing barges down the Mississippi with the current behind her.
Can she hold still and wait?
The current is carrying her along.
The upbound boat can simply ease her throttles and hold her place.
So the vessel with less control gets the say.
You may never run a river, but when a question says downbound with a following current, you’ll know who’s in charge.
